title: Participle vs Gerund — How to Tell Them Apart in 10 Seconds
excerpt: Both end in -ing. Both look identical on paper. Yet 'the crying child' and 'the crying of the child' test two completely different grammar rules. Here is the 10-second test that ends the confusion for good.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Two words. Same -ing ending. Completely different jobs. 'The crying child needs help' and 'Crying doesn't solve problems' both use 'crying' — but one is a participle and one is a gerund, and mixing them up is one of the quietest mark-killers in SSC CGL and Bank PO error-spotting. Most students never learn a real test for telling them apart. They just guess by feel — and the exam is built to punish exactly that guess.

Quick Answer: A gerund is an -ing word acting as a noun (Swimming is fun). A participle is an -ing or -ed word acting as an adjective, describing a noun, or helping form a tense (The swimming boy / She is swimming / The broken chair). The 10-second test: try replacing the -ing word with "something" or "it". If the sentence still makes sense, it's a gerund. If it doesn't, it's a participle.

Why Participle vs Gerund Feels Harder Than It Is

Here's what I've noticed after two decades of teaching this exact topic: students don't struggle with the definitions. Almost everyone can say "gerund is a noun, participle is an adjective" on command. What breaks down is applying that definition to an actual exam sentence in real time, especially when the -ing word sits right next to a noun and could plausibly be either.

  • You see an -ing word and label it a gerund automatically, without checking what job it is doing.
  • You confuse a participle describing a noun with a gerund naming an activity, especially in error-spotting options.
  • You forget that participles also form continuous tenses (is running) and passive/perfect structures (broken glass), not just adjectives.
  • You've never used a fixed test — you decide by "feel", and feel fails under exam pressure.
  • I know exactly how that feels — I watched this exact mix-up cost sharp students marks for years before I started teaching one simple substitution test instead of long definitions.

But here's what most people get wrong: they try to memorise the theory harder, instead of learning one quick test that settles the question in ten seconds flat.

3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks

1. Calling every -ing word a gerund.
Students see "running" and instantly think "noun". But in "The running man crossed the road", running describes man — that's a participle, not a gerund.

2. Treating a participle as if it can take an object like a gerund can.
Gerunds can behave like nouns and take objects in a noun-phrase sense (Reading novels relaxes me). Participles describing a noun cannot be swapped for a plain noun phrase the same way, and forcing that swap creates an unnatural, wrong sentence.

3. Missing participles inside verb tenses altogether.
Students hunt for participles only in adjective positions and completely miss that "is working", "was singing", and "has broken" all contain participles doing tense-forming work, not noun work.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Calling every -ing word a gerund

If the -ing word describes a noun, it is a participle, not a gerund.

Wrong: In "The running man", running is a gerund.

Correct: "Running" here is a present participle describing man.

❌
Mistake 2: Forcing a gerund-style swap onto a participle

A participle describing a noun cannot be turned into an -of phrase like a gerund can.

Wrong: I saw the crying of the child.

Correct: I saw the crying child.

❌
Mistake 3: Missing participles inside verb tenses

"Is working" and "has broken" both contain participles, not gerunds.

Wrong: In "She is working late", working is a gerund.

Correct: "Working" is a present participle completing the continuous tense.

The Complete Participle vs Gerund System, Step by Step

Stop deciding by feel. Run every -ing word through this fixed order, and the answer becomes obvious in seconds.

FormJob in the Sentence10-Second Test
Gerund (-ing)Acts as a noun (subject, object, after preposition)Can you replace it with "something" or "it"?
Present Participle (-ing)Describes a noun, or completes a continuous tenseDoes it sit next to a noun it describes, or follow is/was/am/are/were?
Past Participle (-ed/-en/-t)Describes a noun, or completes perfect/passive tenseDoes it follow has/have/had, or describe a finished state?

Step 1: Find the -ing word and ask what job it is doing. Is it standing in a noun's position, or sitting beside a noun to describe it?

❌ Swimming the boy dived into the pool. (unclear job)
✅ Swimming is good exercise. (gerund — subject, a noun's job)

Step 2: Apply the "something/it" substitution test. If the sentence still makes sense with the -ing word replaced by "something" or "it", it's a gerund.

❌ The crying man annoyed everyone → "The something man annoyed everyone." (fails — so NOT a gerund)
✅ I enjoy reading → "I enjoy something." (test passes — reading is a gerund)

Step 3: Check if the -ing word sits directly beside a noun it describes. If yes, it is almost always a participle, functioning as an adjective.

❌ The sleeping is a child. (sleeping cannot be the naming word here)
✅ The sleeping child did not wake up. (participle describing child)

Step 4: Check if the -ing or -ed word follows a form of "be" or "have". After is/was/am/are/were, an -ing word is a present participle completing a continuous tense. After has/have/had, an -ed/-en word is a past participle completing a perfect tense.

❌ She has broken is a gerund in "She has broken the vase."
✅ She has broken the vase. (past participle completing present perfect tense)

Step 5: Watch for gerunds after prepositions. Any -ing word directly after a preposition (in, at, by, of, without, before, after) is a gerund, never a participle.

❌ He left without saying is a participle.
✅ He left without saying a word. (gerund — noun's job after preposition "without")

Step 6: For introductory -ing phrases at the start of a sentence, check what the phrase describes. This is the classic dangling-modifier trap, and it's always a participle construction, never a gerund one.

❌ Entering the room, the lights went out. (lights did not enter the room)
✅ Entering the room, I switched on the lights. (participle correctly describing "I")

Step-by-Step Strategy

1
Ask what job the -ing word does

Noun's job → gerund. Describing a noun → participle.

Example: Swimming is good exercise.

2
Run the something/it test

If it still makes sense, it's a gerund.

Example: I enjoy reading → I enjoy something.

3
Check if it sits beside a noun it describes

That placement almost always signals a participle.

Example: The sleeping child.

4
Check for be/have before it

After be → continuous tense. After have → perfect tense.

Example: She has broken the vase.

5
Watch for gerunds after prepositions

Always a gerund, never a participle.

Example: He left without saying a word.

6
Check introductory -ing phrases for dangling errors

The phrase must describe the very next subject.

Example: Entering the room, I switched on the lights.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Q1. What is the fastest way to tell a gerund from a participle?
Try replacing the -ing word with "something" or "it". If the sentence still makes sense, it is a gerund. If it doesn't, it is a participle.
Q2. Can the same -ing word be both a gerund and a participle in different sentences?
Yes. The same word like "running" can be a gerund (Running is fun) or a participle (The running man) depending entirely on the job it does in that specific sentence.
Q3. Is the -ing word in a continuous tense a gerund or a participle?
It is a present participle. In "She is working", "working" completes the continuous tense — it is not acting as a noun, so it is not a gerund.
Q4. What is a dangling participle and how does it relate to this topic?
A dangling participle is an introductory -ing phrase that ends up describing the wrong noun, because the phrase and the following subject don't match logically, as in "Entering the room, the lights went out."
Q5. Are -ing words after prepositions always gerunds?
Yes. Any -ing word directly following a preposition such as in, at, by, of, without, or before is always a gerund, never a participle.

title: Gerund or Infinitive After Verb? The Complete List for Bank PO Exams
excerpt: Most aspirants lose marks on gerund vs infinitive questions because they memorise long lists instead of learning the patterns examiners actually test. Here is the complete, exam-ready system with the high-frequency verbs and clear decision rules for SSC CGL and Bank PO.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Gerund or infinitive after a verb? This single choice quietly costs SSC CGL and Bank PO aspirants more marks than almost any other grammar point. Not because the forms are difficult, but because textbooks give long memorisation lists instead of the clear patterns that examiners actually test. Once you see the system behind the lists, the confusion disappears.

Quick Answer: After certain verbs we use only the gerund (-ing), after others only the infinitive (to + verb), and after a small group both forms are possible but the meaning changes. Mastering these three groups is enough for almost every exam question.

Why Gerund vs Infinitive Feels Harder Than It Is

Here's what I've noticed after two decades of teaching this exact topic: students can recite “enjoy takes gerund” and “want takes infinitive”, yet they still choose the wrong form when the sentence looks slightly different or when a verb can take both. The real problem is not memory — it is the lack of a clear decision order.

  • You know many verbs but freeze when you meet a new one in the exam.
  • You mix up the verbs that change meaning with gerund and infinitive.
  • You rely on what “sounds right” in spoken Indian English, which is often wrong in written exams.
  • You have never grouped the verbs into the three practical categories examiners use.
  • I know exactly how that feels — I watched this confusion cost students marks for 22 years before I started teaching the forms as three clear groups instead of one long list.

But here's what most people get wrong: they try to memorise every verb separately instead of learning the three patterns that cover almost every question.

3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks

1. Using infinitive after gerund-only verbs.
Verbs such as enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, keep, practise and suggest are followed only by the gerund. Adding “to” is one of the most common errors in Bank PO papers.

2. Using gerund after infinitive-only verbs.
Verbs such as want, decide, hope, plan, refuse, learn and promise take only the infinitive. Students often put -ing out of habit.

3. Ignoring the meaning change with dual verbs.
Stop, remember, forget, try, regret and go on change meaning depending on the form that follows. Examiners test this distinction every year.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Infinitive after gerund-only verbs

Enjoy, finish, avoid, mind and keep never take the infinitive.

Wrong: She enjoys to read before bed.

Correct: She enjoys reading before bed.

❌
Mistake 2: Gerund after infinitive-only verbs

Want, decide, hope, plan and promise take only the infinitive.

Wrong: He decided applying for the post.

Correct: He decided to apply for the post.

❌
Mistake 3: Ignoring meaning change

Stop + gerund and stop + infinitive mean completely different things.

Wrong: He stopped to smoke (when you mean he quit).

Correct: He stopped smoking (he quit the habit).

Infinitive onlyto + verbwant, decide, hope, plan, refuse, learn, promise, agree, afford, manage

Step 1: Identify whether the verb belongs to the gerund-only group. If it does, never use the infinitive.

❌ She avoids to speak in public.
✅ She avoids speaking in public. (avoid takes only gerund)

Step 2: Check for the infinitive-only group. Want, decide, hope, plan and similar verbs are followed only by to + verb.

❌ They hope getting good marks.
✅ They hope to get good marks. (hope takes only infinitive)

Step 3: Master the dual verbs that change meaning. These are the highest-value questions in the exam.

❌ I remember to lock the door (when you mean a past memory).
✅ I remember locking the door. (memory of a past action)

Step 4: Learn the fixed phrases that always take gerund. look forward to, be used to, object to, prefer + -ing, feel like + -ing.

Step 5: Use infinitive of purpose when the sentence shows why someone does something.

❌ He went to the market for buying vegetables.
✅ He went to the market to buy vegetables. (purpose)

Step 6: Practise the high-frequency pairs that appear in almost every paper.

Three forms. One verb. Endless confusion. Gerunds, infinitives and participles quietly cost SSC CGL and Bank PO aspirants marks every year because most students learn them as three separate lists instead of one clear decision system. Once you see which form the sentence actually needs, the guessing stops.

Quick Answer: A gerund is the -ing form used as a noun (Swimming is good). An infinitive is to + base verb used as noun, adjective or adverb (I want to swim). A participle is the -ing or -ed form used as an adjective or to form continuous/perfect tenses (The swimming boy / The broken chair).

Why Gerunds, Infinitives and Participles Feel Harder Than They Are

Here's what I've noticed after two decades of teaching this exact topic: students do not struggle with the names. Almost everyone can say "gerund ends with -ing". What breaks down is choosing the right form when the sentence gives no clear signal, or when two forms look possible.

  • You know the definitions but freeze when a verb can take both gerund and infinitive with different meanings.
  • You use "to + verb" everywhere because it feels safer, even when the gerund is required.
  • You confuse the present participle (adjective or continuous tense) with the gerund (noun).
  • You have never seen one simple decision order that works for almost every exam question.

But here's what most people get wrong: they try to memorise long lists of verbs that take gerunds or infinitives, instead of learning the purpose each form serves in the sentence.

3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks

1. Using infinitive after verbs that only take gerunds.
Verbs like enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, keep and practise are followed by the gerund, not the infinitive. Students often add "to" out of habit and lose easy marks.

2. Treating every -ing word as a gerund.
The -ing form can be a gerund (noun) or a present participle (adjective or part of continuous tense). Mixing the two leads to wrong sentence correction answers.

3. Ignoring meaning change with verbs that take both forms.
Verbs like stop, remember, forget and try change meaning depending on whether a gerund or infinitive follows. Examiners love these traps.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Infinitive after gerund-only verbs

Enjoy, finish, avoid, mind and keep take only the gerund.

Wrong: She enjoys to read novels.

Correct: She enjoys reading novels.

❌
Mistake 2: Calling every -ing form a gerund

If the -ing word describes a noun, it is a participle, not a gerund.

Wrong: The running man is a gerund.

Correct: The running man — "running" is a present participle.

❌
Mistake 3: Ignoring meaning change

Stop + gerund and stop + infinitive mean different things.

Wrong: He stopped to smoke (when you mean he quit the habit).

Correct: He stopped smoking (he quit the habit).

Describes a noun → participle. Names an activity → gerund.

Example: the sleeping child (participle)

Use infinitive for purpose

When the sentence answers "why", choose the infinitive.

look forward to + gerund, want + infinitive, keep + gerund.

The Real Reason Tense Errors Keep Catching You

Here's what I've noticed after two decades of teaching this exact topic:

  • You read the sentence and pick the tense that “feels correct” instead of checking the time words.
  • You mix present perfect and simple past because both talk about past actions.
  • You forget that “since” and “for” force present perfect, while “ago” forces simple past.
  • You change a correct verb because the rest of the sentence looks complicated.

But here's what most people get wrong: they treat tense as a memory topic. It is not. It is a matching game between time signals and verb forms.

Three Mistakes That Cost Marks Every Year

1. Ignoring the time marker.
Students focus on the main verb and forget the small words that decide the tense. “Yesterday”, “last week”, “ago”, “since”, “already” are not decoration — they are instructions.

2. Confusing completed action with ongoing action.
Simple past shows a finished action. Present perfect shows a past action that still connects to now. Mixing them is the single biggest source of wrong answers.

3. Changing the correct form because of subject-verb agreement noise.
When the sentence is long, students start fixing number agreement and accidentally change a correct tense. The two errors are separate.

Both talk about past, but one needs a finished time and the other does not.

Wrong: I finished my work just now.

Correct: I have just finished my work.

❌

Long sentences make you over-edit.

The Logic of Participle Clauses

When an introductory participle phrase (starting with a V-ing or V3) opens a sentence, it borrows its grammatical subject from the noun immediately following the comma.

❌ Being a rainy day, I decided to stay indoors.
✅ It being a rainy day, I decided to stay indoors. (or: As it was a rainy day, I decided to stay indoors.)

title: 12 Tenses in English Grammar with Examples — Complete Chart for SSC CGL 2026
excerpt: Most aspirants can recite tense names but freeze the moment an exam mixes two tenses in one sentence. Here is the complete 12-tense chart with exam-style examples, organized the way examiners actually test it — not the way textbooks teach it.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Twelve tenses. That's it. Not fifteen, not twenty — just twelve, and yet this single topic quietly costs SSC CGL and Bank PO aspirants more marks than almost any other grammar area. Not because the tenses themselves are hard, but because textbooks teach them as twelve separate boxes instead of one connected system. Once you see the pattern behind the twelve, error spotting and sentence correction questions stop feeling like guesswork.

Quick Answer: English has 12 tenses, built from 3 time frames (present, past, future) crossed with 4 aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous). Every tense question in SSC CGL and Bank PO exams tests one of these 12 combinations, and mastering the time-plus-aspect grid removes the need to memorize each tense in isolation.

Table of Contents

  1. Why Tenses Feel Harder Than They Are
  2. 3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks
  3. The Complete 12-Tense Chart, Step by Step
  4. A Quick Turnaround Story
  5. Expert Tips From the Classroom
  6. Frequently Asked Questions

Why Tenses Feel Harder Than They Are

Here's what I've noticed after two decades of teaching this exact topic: students don't actually struggle with individual tenses. Almost everyone can correctly say 'I am eating' versus 'I ate'. What breaks down is switching between tenses inside a single sentence, or recognizing which tense a sentence needs when a time-clue word like 'since', 'for', or 'by the time' is hiding in the middle of it.

  • You know the tense names, but freeze when a sentence has no obvious time word.
  • You confuse Present Perfect ('I have finished') with Simple Past ('I finished') because both feel "already done".
  • You've never seen all 12 tenses laid out in one single chart, only scattered across different chapters.
  • You get the base tense right but miss the aspect (continuous vs perfect) under exam time pressure.
  • I know exactly how that feels — I watched this exact confusion play out in my classroom for 22 years before I started teaching tenses as one connected grid instead of twelve separate rules.

But here's what most people get wrong: they try to learn each tense as an isolated rule with its own examples, instead of learning the underlying 3-by-4 grid that generates all twelve automatically.

3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks

1. Treating 'since' and 'for' as interchangeable.
Both words signal Present Perfect or Present Perfect Continuous, but they attach to completely different types of time reference. 'Since' pairs with a starting point in time ('since 2020', 'since Monday'), while 'for' pairs with a duration ('for five years', 'for two hours'). Mixing them up is one of the most common Bank PO cloze-test errors.

2. Using Simple Past when Present Perfect is required.
'I have submitted the form' and 'I submitted the form' look similar but mean different things to an examiner. Present Perfect connects the past action to the present moment (the form is submitted now, right now), while Simple Past simply states a completed past event with no connection to now. Sentence Improvement questions test this distinction constantly.

3. Forgetting that Future Continuous and Future Perfect exist as separate exam categories.
Most students memorize Simple Future ('I will go') and stop there, completely skipping Future Continuous ('I will be going') and Future Perfect ('I will have gone'). These two account for a small but consistent share of error-spotting questions every single year, precisely because so few aspirants revise them.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Confusing 'since' with 'for'

'Since' needs a starting point; 'for' needs a duration — they are not interchangeable.

Wrong: I have lived here for 2020.

Correct: I have lived here since 2020.

❌
Mistake 2: Simple Past instead of Present Perfect

Present Perfect links a past action to right now; Simple Past does not.

Wrong: I submitted the form (implying it's done and relevant now).

Correct: I have submitted the form.

❌
Mistake 3: Ignoring Future Continuous and Future Perfect

Most revision stops at Simple Future, skipping two full exam-tested tenses.

Wrong: By next year, I will complete the course.

Correct: By next year, I will have completed the course.

The Complete 12-Tense Chart, Step by Step

Instead of memorizing 12 unrelated rules, think of English tense as one grid: 3 time-frames (Present, Past, Future) multiplied by 4 aspects (Simple, Continuous, Perfect, Perfect Continuous). Once this grid is in your head, you can construct any tense on demand instead of recalling it from memory.

AspectPresentPastFuture
SimpleI writeI wroteI will write
ContinuousI am writingI was writingI will be writing
PerfectI have writtenI had writtenI will have written
Perfect ContinuousI have been writingI had been writingI will have been writing

Step 1: Master the 4 Present tenses first. These appear most frequently in error-spotting questions because they interact with 'since/for' and habitual-action clues.

❌ She is knowing the answer.
✅ She knows the answer. (stative verbs like 'know' never take continuous form)

Step 2: Learn the 4 Past tenses as a timeline, not as isolated forms. Simple Past states a fact, Past Continuous shows an action in progress, Past Perfect shows an action completed before another past action, and Past Perfect Continuous shows a duration leading up to a past moment.

❌ When I reached the station, the train left.
✅ When I reached the station, the train had left. (the earlier of two past actions must take Past Perfect)

Step 3: Treat the 4 Future tenses as predictions, plans, and deadlines. Simple Future is a plain prediction, Future Continuous shows an action in progress at a future point, Future Perfect shows completion by a deadline, and Future Perfect Continuous shows an ongoing duration up to a future point.

Step 4: Attach fixed time-markers to each aspect, and let the marker decide the tense for you. This is the single highest-leverage exam strategy in this entire topic.

Time MarkerTense It Signals
since, for, already, just, yet, ever, neverPresent Perfect
yesterday, ago, last week, in [past year]Simple Past
by the time, before, after (past context)Past Perfect
by tomorrow, by next year, by the time (future context)Future Perfect

Step 5: Practice sentence-correction questions that mix two tenses in one sentence. This is exactly how SSC CGL and IBPS PO test this topic — never in isolation, always in combination.

❌ She has completed her degree three years ago.
✅ She completed her degree three years ago. (a specific past time marker like 'three years ago' always overrides Present Perfect)

Step 6: Test stative verbs separately, since they break the continuous-form pattern entirely. Verbs like know, believe, own, love, and want do not take continuous forms even when the sentence describes an ongoing state.

Step-by-Step Strategy

1
Master the 4 Present Tenses First

Highest-frequency tense group in error-spotting questions.

Example: She knows the answer (not 'is knowing').

2
Learn Past Tenses as a Timeline

The earlier of two past actions always takes Past Perfect.

Example: When I reached, the train had left.

3
Treat Future Tenses as Predictions & Deadlines

Four future forms, not just Simple Future.

4
Attach Fixed Time-Markers to Each Aspect

Let the time-marker word decide the tense for you.

Example: 'since 2020' always signals Present Perfect.

5
Practice Mixed-Tense Sentences

Exams never test one tense alone — always in combination.

Example: She completed her degree three years ago (not 'has completed').

6
Test Stative Verbs Separately

Know, believe, own, love, want never take continuous forms.

title: Gerund or Infinitive After Verb? The Complete List for Bank PO Exams
excerpt: Eight out of ten Bank PO aspirants lose easy marks not because they don't know grammar — but because they guess between 'enjoy swimming' and 'enjoy to swim' by ear. Here is the complete, memorizable list that ends the guessing forever.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Stop guessing. That's the first thing I tell every batch. 'I enjoy swimming' is correct. 'I enjoy to swim' is not. And no, it's not because 'swimming' sounds nicer — it's because 'enjoy' belongs to a fixed list of verbs that only accept a gerund, never an infinitive. If you've ever second-guessed yourself between 'want to go' and 'want going' in the middle of a Bank PO paper, this post is going to fix that confusion permanently.

Quick Answer: Some verbs in English (like enjoy, avoid, and finish) are always followed by a gerund (V-ing), while others (like want, decide, and hope) are always followed by an infinitive (to + verb). There is no shortcut around memorizing which verb belongs to which group — but a list of the 40 highest-frequency exam verbs, sorted by pattern, makes the job manageable in a single sitting.

Why This Trips Up Even Strong Students

Here's the part nobody tells you in a regular classroom: gerund-versus-infinitive isn't really a grammar rule in the way subject-verb agreement is. There's no logical test you can apply mid-exam. It's a matter of which verbs, by convention, "go with" which structure — and that convention has to be memorized, not derived.

This is exactly why so many aspirants who are otherwise strong in tenses and articles still stumble here. They're looking for a rule where there is only a pattern. And in a 60-second-per-question exam like IBPS PO Prelims, there's no time to sit and reason it out — you either know the verb's pattern instantly, or you lose the mark.

  • You've memorized 10-15 verbs, but the exam picks the one you missed.
  • You confuse 'stop to do' with 'stop doing' — and they mean completely different things.
  • You freeze on verbs like 'like', 'love', 'prefer' that can technically take both, but shift meaning slightly.
  • You've never seen the full list organized by pattern, only scattered examples in different books.

But here's what most people get wrong: they try to memorize gerund/infinitive rules through isolated sentences instead of grouped lists. Grouping is what makes this stick.

The 3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks

Mistake 1: Treating 'stop', 'remember', and 'try' like fixed-pattern verbs.
These three are the most dangerous verbs in this entire topic because they change meaning depending on which form follows them. 'I stopped to smoke' means I paused another activity in order to smoke. 'I stopped smoking' means I quit the habit entirely. Students memorize one version and apply it everywhere — and lose marks on both.

Mistake 2: Assuming 'suggest' takes an infinitive because it "feels" like a request.
'Suggest' is a gerund-only verb — 'He suggested going early', never 'he suggested to go early'. Aspirants confuse it with 'want' or 'advise', which do take infinitives, because all three verbs semantically involve telling someone to do something.

Mistake 3: Forgetting that a preposition before a verb always forces a gerund.
'Look forward to', 'good at', 'interested in' — whenever a preposition sits directly before a verb, that verb must be in the -ing form, no exceptions. 'I am interested to learn' is a very common wrong answer choice in Bank PO papers specifically because it sounds acceptable in spoken English.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Treating 'stop' as a fixed-pattern verb

'Stop + infinitive' and 'stop + gerund' mean completely different things.

Wrong meaning mix-up: I stopped to smoke = quit smoking (INCORRECT)

Correct: I stopped smoking = quit the habit

❌
Mistake 2: Giving 'suggest' an infinitive

'Suggest' is gerund-only, confused with request verbs like 'advise'.

Wrong: He suggested to go early.

Correct: He suggested going early.

❌
Mistake 3: Forgetting the preposition-forces-gerund rule

A preposition right before a verb always forces the -ing form.

Wrong: I am interested to learn.

Correct: I am interested in learning.

The Solution: 5 Grouped Lists That Actually Stick

Step 1: Memorize the Gerund-Only Group First.
These 12 verbs are always followed by V-ing and never by 'to + verb': enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, admit, deny, mind, risk, postpone, delay, practice, resist. Read them out loud as a chant three times a day for a week — this single group covers roughly 30% of gerund/infinitive questions in SSC and Bank exams.

❌ She admitted to steal the documents.
✅ She admitted stealing the documents.

Step 2: Memorize the Infinitive-Only Group Second.
These 12 verbs are always followed by 'to + verb': want, decide, hope, plan, promise, refuse, agree, manage, afford, fail, offer, seem.

❌ He refused signing the form.
✅ He refused to sign the form.

Step 3: Isolate the Meaning-Changing Verbs.
Only four verbs genuinely change meaning depending on the form used: stop, remember, forget, try. Learn these as pairs, not as a single rule — because a single rule will actively mislead you here.

  • Remember to lock the door (don't forget to do it — future obligation) vs Remember locking the door (recall having done it — past memory)
  • Try to open the jar (attempt something difficult) vs Try opening the jar under hot water (experiment with a method)

Step 4: Learn the Preposition-Forces-Gerund Rule as a Single Universal Law.
Whenever 'to' functions as a preposition rather than part of an infinitive, it must be followed by a gerund. This covers 'look forward to', 'object to', 'used to' (in the habitual sense), 'with a view to', 'in addition to', and every adjective + preposition combination like 'good at', 'keen on', 'interested in'.

❌ I look forward to meet you.
✅ I look forward to meeting you.

Step 5: Drill With Real Sentence Completion Format Under Time Pressure.
Grammar knowledge that only exists on paper doesn't transfer to a 60-second exam question. Once you know the four groups, time yourself doing 20 fill-in-the-blank questions in under 8 minutes. Speed under pressure is what separates knowing the rule from being able to use it.

Step-by-Step Strategy

1
Memorize the Gerund-Only Group

enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, admit, deny, mind, risk, postpone, delay, practice, resist.

Example: She admitted stealing the documents.

2
Memorize the Infinitive-Only Group

want, decide, hope, plan, promise, refuse, agree, manage, afford, fail, offer, seem.

Example: He refused to sign the form.

3
Isolate Meaning-Changing Verbs

stop, remember, forget, try — learn as contrasting pairs, not as one rule.

Example: Remember to lock the door vs Remember locking the door.

4
Apply the Preposition-Forces-Gerund Law

'to' as a preposition, plus every adjective + preposition combo, needs V-ing.

Example: I look forward to meeting you.

5
Drill Under Timed Conditions

Q2. Why do 'stop', 'remember', 'forget', and 'try' behave differently from other verbs?

Q5. Is 'used to' always followed by a gerund?
Only when 'used to' functions as an adjective phrase meaning 'accustomed to' (e.g., 'used to waking up early'). When 'used to' expresses a past habit that no longer continues, it is followed by the base verb, not a gerund (e.g., 'I used to wake up early').

title: Sequence of Tenses Rules for Competitive Exams — Direct & Indirect Speech Explained
excerpt: Why does 'He said he is tired' feel right but score zero in SSC CGL? The Sequence of Tenses rule silently governs every Direct-to-Indirect conversion — and most aspirants have never learned it as a standalone rule. Here is the complete backshift system explained.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Here's a sentence that looks completely normal but is wrong in every competitive exam: 'The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun, and I understand it is a scientific fact.' Wait — that one is actually correct, and it confuses students precisely because it looks like an exception. The real question examiners test again and again is this: when you report someone's words, does the tense of the reported sentence change, stay the same, or depend on something else entirely? The answer is a single, learnable system called the Sequence of Tenses — and once you see the pattern, Direct and Indirect Speech questions stop being guesswork.

📊 Topic Weightage in Competitive Exams

Exam NameQuestion TypesAverage Marks
SSC CGL (Tier 1 & Tier 2)Direct-Indirect Conversion, Error Spotting3 - 5 Marks
IBPS PO / SBI POSentence Rearrangement, Cloze Test2 - 4 Marks
UPSC CDS / NDAReported Speech Conversion2 - 3 Marks
Railways (RRB) / State PSCGrammar Objective Section2 - 3 Marks

What 'Sequence of Tenses' Actually Means

The Sequence of Tenses rule governs how the tense of a subordinate clause (like the reported speech inside quotation marks) relates to the tense of the main reporting verb (said, told, asked). It has nothing to do with punctuation or reporting verbs like 'says' versus 'said' in isolation — it is entirely about one question: is the reporting verb in the past tense or not? That single fact decides almost everything else.

Rule 1: Reporting Verb in Past Tense — The Universal Backshift

When the reporting verb ('said', 'told') is in the past tense, the tense inside the reported speech generally shifts one step back into the past. This is called backshift, and it is the single most tested rule in this topic.

❌ He said that he is going to Mumbai tomorrow.
✅ He said that he was going to Mumbai the next day.

Here is the complete backshift chart used in every exam:

Direct Speech TenseIndirect Speech TenseExample
Simple PresentSimple Past'I play' → he said he played
Present ContinuousPast Continuous'I am playing' → he said he was playing
Present PerfectPast Perfect'I have played' → he said he had played
Simple PastPast Perfect'I played' → he said he had played
WillWould'I will play' → he said he would play
CanCould'I can play' → he said he could play

Rule 2: The 'Universal Truth' Exception

This is the exception that trips up the most confident students. When the reported statement is a universal fact, scientific truth, or habitual action, the tense inside the reported speech does NOT change, even if the reporting verb is in the past.

❌ The teacher said that water boiled at 100 degrees Celsius.
✅ The teacher said that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
  • ✅ He said that honesty is the best policy. (universal truth)
  • ✅ She told me that she goes for a walk every morning. (habitual action, often kept in present)

Rule 3: Reporting Verb in Present or Future — No Backshift Needed

If the reporting verb is in the present or future tense ('says', 'will say'), the tense of the reported speech stays exactly as it was in the original sentence. No backshift applies at all.

❌ He says that he was busy right now.
✅ He says that he is busy right now.

Rule 4: Modal Verbs That Never Change

Certain modal verbs stay exactly the same in Indirect Speech regardless of the reporting verb's tense, because they already express a fixed or unconditional idea: could, would, should, might, ought to, must (for obligation), used to.

  • ✅ He said, 'I could help you.' → He said that he could help me.
  • ✅ She said, 'You should apologize.' → She said that I should apologize.

Rule 5: Pronoun and Time-Word Changes That Accompany Tense Shift

Sequence of Tenses questions almost never appear alone — examiners pair them with pronoun and adverb-of-time changes to test whether you can juggle multiple rules at once.

Direct SpeechIndirect Speech
nowthen
todaythat day
tomorrowthe next day / the following day
yesterdaythe previous day / the day before
thisthat
herethere
❌ She said, 'I will finish this today.' → She said she would finish this today.
✅ She said, 'I will finish this today.' → She said she would finish that day.

Rule 6: Interrogative and Imperative Sentences Follow the Same Backshift Logic

Questions and commands are not exempt from Sequence of Tenses — they simply add their own structural change on top of the same backshift rule.

  • ✅ He asked, 'Are you coming?' → He asked if I was coming. (backshift still applies)
  • ✅ She said, 'Close the door.' → She told me to close the door. (imperatives use infinitive, not tense backshift, but the reporting verb still governs formality)

title: Articles Before Vowel Sounds — Why 'An Hour' Is Correct But 'A Hour' Is Wrong
excerpt: Still choosing 'a' or 'an' by looking at the first letter? That's the trap. The real rule is about sound, not spelling — and this one mistake costs students marks in Class 12 boards and every major competitive exam.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Here's a mistake I've corrected in my classroom for over two decades: students choose 'a' or 'an' by looking at the letter a word starts with. That's not the rule. The real rule depends on the sound, not the spelling — and once you understand this, traps like 'an hour', 'a university', and 'an MBA' stop being traps.

📊 Topic Weightage in Competitive Exams

Exam NameQuestion TypesAverage Marks

The Real Rule: Sound, Not Spelling

Use 'an' before words that begin with a vowel sound (regardless of the first letter), and 'a' before words that begin with a consonant sound (regardless of the first letter).

❌ She waited for a hour before her interview.
✅ She waited for an hour before her interview. (the 'h' is silent, so the word starts with the vowel sound 'ow')

Rule 1: The Silent 'H' Trap

When 'h' at the start of a word is silent, the word begins with a vowel sound — so it takes 'an'.

  • ✅ He is an honest man. (silent h)
  • ✅ She is an heir to the family business. (silent h)
  • ✅ It took an hour to reach the station. (silent h)
  • Compare: He gave a heavy sigh. (the 'h' in 'heavy' IS pronounced, so it takes 'a')

Rule 2: Words Starting With 'U' or 'EU' That Sound Like 'Yoo'

Some words spelled with a vowel actually start with a consonant sound ('y'), so they take 'a', not 'an'.

❌ He studies at an university in Pune.
✅ He studies at a university in Pune. (sounds like 'yoo-niversity')
  • ✅ A unanimous decision was taken.
  • ✅ A European delegation visited the campus.
  • ✅ A one-rupee coin. (starts with the 'w' sound — 'won')

Rule 3: Abbreviations and Acronyms — Read the First Letter's Sound

For abbreviations, don't look at the letter — say the letter's name out loud and check if that name starts with a vowel sound.

  • ✅ She has an MBA degree. ('M' is pronounced 'em' — vowel sound)
  • ✅ He cleared an SSC exam last year. ('S' is pronounced 'es' — vowel sound)
  • ✅ He worked for a UN agency. ('U' here is pronounced 'yoo' — consonant sound)

Always the sound. A word that starts with a vowel letter but a consonant sound (like 'university') takes 'a', and a word that starts with a consonant letter but a vowel sound (like 'hour') takes 'an'.
Q2. Why is it 'an hour' but 'a horse'?
In 'hour', the 'h' is silent, so the word is pronounced starting with the vowel sound 'ow'. In 'horse', the 'h' is clearly pronounced, so it starts with a consonant sound and takes 'a'.
Q3. How do I decide the article for an abbreviation like 'MBA' or 'SSC'?
Say the first letter's name aloud, not the full word. 'M' sounds like 'em' (vowel sound, so 'an MBA'), while 'S' sounds like 'es' (vowel sound, so 'an SSC').

title: Conditional Sentences: How SSC & IBPS Trick You With 'Had + Would Have' Traps
excerpt: Why do exam boards repeat the Third Conditional error every single year? Because students keep placing 'would have' inside the 'if-clause'. Here is the foolproof formula to lock in full marks.
author: ZeroErrorEnglish Editorial Team
content:
If there is one grammar topic that has appeared consistently in every SSC CGL, CHSL, and Bank PO exam over the past fifteen years, it is Conditional Sentences. Yet year after year, aspirants lose 2 to 4 easy marks because they memorize rules in isolation without mastering the structure pairings.

📊 Exam Frequency Overview

ExamFormatFrequency
SSC CGL Tier 1 & 2Sentence Improvement & Error Spotting2 - 3 Questions every shift
IBPS PO / ClerkFill in the blanks & Cloze TestHigh frequency in Mains
UPSC CDS / NDASentence Completion1 - 2 Questions

The Golden Law of Conditionals

Let's establish the non-negotiable fundamental rule first:

Rule: The 'If-clause' (subordinate conditional clause) can NEVER contain modal auxiliaries like will, shall, would, could, might, or would have.

The 4 Conditional Types at a Glance

TypeIf Clause (Condition)Main Clause (Result)Example
ZeroSimple Present (V1)Simple Present (V1)If you heat ice, it melts.
FirstSimple Present (V1 / does)will / can / may + V1If he studies hard, he will clear the cutoff.
SecondSimple Past (V2 / were)would / could + V1If I were you, I would take the mock test.
ThirdPast Perfect (had + V3)would have + V3If she had revised the rules, she would have scored full marks.

The #1 Trap: 'Had + Would Have' in the If-Clause

Examiners love writing sentences like this:

❌ If you would have informed me earlier, I would have accompanied you to the center.
✅ If you had informed me earlier, I would have accompanied you to the center.

Remember: In the 3rd conditional, the action that happened first in past time takes had + V3, while the hypothetical consequence takes would have + V3. Never duplicate 'would have'!

Inverted Conditionals (Without 'If')

In high-level exams like IBPS PO Mains and UPSC CSAT, examiners omit the word 'if' altogether to test your syntactic awareness:

  • Normal 3rd conditional: If he had invited us, we would have attended.
  • Inverted form: Had he invited us, we would have attended.
  • Subjunctive 2nd conditional: Were I the chairman, I would reform the syllabus.

title: Subject-Verb Agreement in Inverted Sentences: The 3-Second Bracket Rule That Never Fails
excerpt: Ever stared at an error-spotting question starting with 'Hardly', 'Seldom', or 'Along the river bank', and wondered why your gut feeling failed you? Here is the bracket-elimination technique my classroom students have used for 22 years.
author: ZeroErrorEnglish Editorial Team
content:
Ever noticed how easy Subject-Verb Agreement feels until the examiner flips the sentence order on you? In normal English, the subject comes first, followed by the verb. But in competitive exams like SSC CGL, IBPS PO, and UPSC CDS, examiners intentionally hide the real subject behind long prepositional phrases or negative adverbs. The result? 70% of candidates pick the wrong option based purely on 'what sounds right'.

📊 Topic Weightage in Competitive Exams

Exam NameQuestion TypesAverage Marks
SSC CGL (Tier 1 & Tier 2)Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement4 - 6 Marks
IBPS PO / SBI POError Detection, Phrase Replacement3 - 5 Marks
UPSC CDS / NDASpotting Errors3 - 4 Marks
State PSC (MPSC, UPPSC)Grammar Objective Section2 - 4 Marks

The Real Culprit: Why Your Ear Betrays You

Consider this sentence from a recent SSC CGL Tier 1 paper:

"Along the northern borders of the country lies the majestic Himalayan peaks." (Spot the error)

If you read this quickly, your ear catches 'country' right before 'lies'. Since 'country' is singular, 'lies' sounds perfectly natural. But that's the trap! The country isn't lying anywhere. What is lying along the borders? 'The majestic Himalayan peaks' — which is plural! The correct verb must be lie.

The 3-Second 'Bracket-Elimination' Method

After 22 years in the classroom, I tell my students to never read an inverted sentence with their ears. Use your pencil and bracket out modifying prepositional phrases:

  1. Step 1: Put brackets around prepositional phrases starting with in, on, at, along, between, among, under.
  2. Step 2: Ask 'Who or What performs the action?' to find the real subject after the verb.
  3. Step 3: Match the verb number directly to that post-positioned subject.
❌ [Along the northern borders] [of the country] lies (Singular Verb) the majestic Himalayan peaks (Plural Subject).
✅ [Along the northern borders] [of the country] lie (Plural Verb) the majestic Himalayan peaks (Plural Subject).

Rule 2: Negative Adverb Inversion (Hardly, Seldom, Never, Scarcely)

When a sentence begins with a negative or restrictive adverb, subject-auxiliary inversion is mandatory:

Formula: Negative Adverb + Auxiliary Verb + Subject + Main Verb

  • ❌ Seldom he visits his ancestral village in summer.
  • ✅ Seldom does he visit his ancestral village in summer.
  • ❌ Hardly I had entered the hall when the bell rang.
  • ✅ Hardly had I entered the hall when the bell rang.

Q1. What is an inverted sentence in English grammar?
An inverted sentence is one where the predicate (verb or auxiliary) appears before the subject, commonly used for emphasis, locational fronting, or after negative adverbs like 'Hardly', 'Rarely', or 'Scarcely'.
Q2. How do I quickly identify the subject in an inverted sentence during exams?
Apply the Bracket Method: mentally put parentheses around all prepositional phrases. Once modifiers are filtered out, locate the noun phrase after the verb that answers 'Who?' or 'What?'.

Yes. Agreement blunders in introductory essay paragraphs or formal letters immediately signal weak grammatical foundation to evaluators, deducting crucial syntax and coherence marks.
